entry.title: When a Directory Is a Queue
entry.content:
Consider a native desktop application that produces reports, recordings, or diagnostic bundles. Those artifacts live on the user's machine first; creating one does not necessarily trigger an upload.

The delay may be deliberate. On a metered connection, uploading immediately may cost more than waiting. An offline-first application also needs to let the user keep working without a reachable server. Cloud delivery is a separate operation that may happen later, after the app has closed and restarted.

When delivery becomes appropriate, a background uploader finds the pending files, uploads them, and deletes the local copies when delivery succeeds. Someone proposes tracking the uploads in a database. Someone else asks why the presence of the file isn't enough.

Both designs can work. Both can lose data if their recovery rules are wrong. I'd choose between them by looking at the delivery state the application needs to track.

A directory already implements a queue

Suppose this application produces a diagnostic report with the identity report-0042. The producer writes report-0042.partial while generating it, then publishes report-0042.ready when it is complete. A background worker scans for ready files, uploads them when eligible, and removes the local copies after delivery succeeds. Failed uploads leave the files in place. On restart, the worker scans again.

The files already give the worker a way to recover pending uploads after a restart:

  • A file in the pending directory represents work to do.
  • Removing it acknowledges completion.
  • Scanning reconstructs pending work after a restart.

It looks like a hack. It probably is one.1 But for a small uploader, it may be a better fit than introducing a separate delivery ledger.2 The file itself is the pending upload; there is no separate queue row pointing to it. For a single-process worker with a modest backlog, repeatable uploads, and no requirement to preserve attempt history, that is a useful reduction in moving parts.

The filename distinguishes an incomplete report from a completed one. It doesn't record when to retry a failed upload, whether delivery has been permanently rejected, or whether the upload succeeded but local deletion failed.3

Those distinctions don't disappear because the design leaves them unnamed.

Separate the facts before choosing the store

There are at least three independent questions:

Question Example
What bytes exist locally? The finalized file report-0042.ready is available on disk.
Is delivery allowed? The report's associated record has been accepted; consent or retention policy permits delivery.
What happened during delivery? The remote service acknowledged report-0042; local cleanup remains.

The database can record whether a report is allowed to upload, while the filesystem holds the report itself. Using both is not a conflict by itself. The problem arises when they record the same fact differently and the app has no rule for deciding which to trust.

A row for report-0042 with its state set to ready can express the application's intention to deliver the report. It cannot guarantee that the file still exists. A user, another process, or a storage failure can invalidate that assumption after the transaction commits.

The distinction matters in the other direction too. A file on disk proves neither authorization to upload nor the existence of the business record it belongs to. Finding an untracked file during a recovery scan is not enough reason to upload it. The app still needs to check whether delivery is allowed.

“Uploaded” is not “deleted”

With file presence as the only delivery state, the worker can repeat an upload indefinitely:

  1. The remote service accepts report-0042.
  2. The client tries to delete report-0042.ready.
  3. Deletion fails.4
  4. The next scan finds the ready file and uploads the report again.

The network operation succeeded. The cleanup operation failed. Treating file presence as the only state collapses those outcomes into “upload pending.”

A small acknowledgement marker can preserve the distinction without introducing a database. After validating the remote acknowledgement, the worker persists report-0042.ack next to the report. Only after the marker is durable does it attempt to delete the payload. Subsequent scans that find the marker retry deletion, not transmission. The marker must identify this immutable report: reusing the same identity for different bytes could let an old acknowledgement suppress a new upload.

For this report, the protocol has five local representations:

  • report-0042.partial: production is incomplete. The uploader skips the incomplete file. The producer may still be writing it; if production was interrupted, recovery code must decide what to do with it.
  • report-0042.ready: the report is finalized and pending delivery. The worker uploads it if eligible.
  • report-0042.ready plus report-0042.ack: delivery is acknowledged and cleanup remains. The worker retries local cleanup.
  • report-0042.ack without the payload: delivery is acknowledged, but the local report is absent. The worker removes the leftover marker.
  • Neither payload nor marker: there is no local work to reconstruct from this directory.

On a filesystem that provides an atomic rename within the same filesystem, the producer can finish and close report-0042.partial, then rename it to report-0042.ready. The worker sees either the incomplete name or the published name, not an intermediate rename state. This is a better completion signal than “the modification time is more than a few seconds old.” An idle writer is not necessarily a finished writer.

Atomic visibility does not guarantee durability across power loss. If surviving power loss is a requirement, the app must also flush file contents and directory changes in the order required by its platform. The same durability requirement applies to the acknowledgement marker.

These filenames and markers form a small filesystem protocol. Different processes and application versions need to interpret them consistently, including files left behind before an upgrade. Changing those conventions requires compatibility and recovery rules, just as changing a database schema does.

The uncertainty window doesn't go away

Once durable, the marker separates a completed upload from unfinished local cleanup. It does not make the remote write and the local acknowledgement atomic.

Suppose the remote service accepts report-0042 and the process crashes before report-0042.ack is durable. On restart, the worker finds report-0042.ready without a marker. The local evidence is indistinguishable from a report that was never delivered.

A database row has the same problem. If the process crashes before committing the report's acknowledgement, the row still says pending. An ordinary local transaction does not include the remote object-store write. Moving the acknowledgement into SQL doesn't remove the gap.

The delivery protocol needs safe retries or a way to determine whether the remote service accepted the report. A stable remote key can make repeated writes of the same immutable report safe, provided overwriting preserves the intended meaning. The server could instead recognize an idempotency key, or retain an upload receipt that the client can look up after a restart. Reusing a key is not sufficient when the bytes can change or each upload triggers additional side effects.

Even safe repetition has a cost. Repeated writes can consume bandwidth, requests, retained object versions, and downstream processing. “The final object is the same” is a correctness property, not a cost model.

Neither storage choice, on its own, guarantees exactly-once delivery.

Delivery state worth querying

A database becomes useful when the app needs to track and query retry times, errors, and which worker is handling each upload.

Suppose the report's next attempt is due in twenty minutes, and that deadline must survive a restart. An operator also needs to see its last error and distinguish a temporary outage from permanent rejection. Adding priorities or several workers introduces more facts to track.

Now the query is no longer “which files remain?” It is “which eligible reports are due, not terminally failed, and not owned by another worker?” An indexed query and a transaction may be substantially simpler than a directory scan plus several kinds of sidecar file.

The report's delivery ledger might contain:

artifact_id
payload_path
state
attempt_count
next_attempt_at
remote_object_key
acknowledged_at
last_error

That isn't a mandatory schema. I would add a lease when workers need coordinated ownership, and attempt history when there is a reason to retain it. The ledger need not become a generic workflow engine.

If the ledger also records an uploading state, it needs a recovery rule for attempts left in that state. With multiple workers, the record alone cannot establish whether the original worker has stopped or another worker may take over.

A lease can help coordinate those claims, but an expired lease doesn't magically stop a slow old worker. The remote protocol still needs to tolerate duplicate or stale attempts.

Transactions, indexes, constraints, and queries can now express the required behavior more directly than a growing filesystem convention does. If the application already has a well-supported local database, the incremental cost may be small. At that point, avoiding one table could mean building its replacement out of sidecar files.

The row/file boundary

Suppose the database stores the upload status and the path to the report, while the report itself remains a separate file. Updating the row and creating or deleting the file are separate operations. A crash between them can leave a file without a row, or a row without a file:

Observed state Required decision
report-0042.ready exists, row absent Is this an orphan or recoverable work?
Row exists, report file absent Can the report be regenerated, or is this a terminal missing-artifact error?
Row says acknowledged, report file exists Retry cleanup, not upload.
Row says pending, remote accepted the report Resolve through the idempotency or receipt protocol.

The answers depend on the domain. Automatically importing every orphan may violate eligibility rules. Automatically deleting every unreferenced file may destroy recoverable work. A generic “reconcile” function isn't a design until those choices are explicit.

If the report contents and upload status are stored in the same database transaction, they can be committed together. The remote upload still happens outside that transaction. Storing the contents in the database changes other tradeoffs: database size, write amplification, backup behavior, streaming, and storage reclamation. For large media artifacts, keeping the bytes as files can still be the better choice.

Processing the backlog

Once the app knows which reports still need delivery, it has another decision to make: how many to upload at once. After a long offline period, it may have thousands of pending reports but capacity for only a few concurrent transfers. Choosing a directory or a database does not set that limit.

A single upload process can keep its list of current transfers in memory and limit itself to four concurrent requests. Its saved records can continue to say “pending” until it records a successful upload. After a crash, it reconstructs pending work and retries safely. The scheduler can enforce that limit over either a directory or a database; storing every pending report in a database does not impose a request limit by itself.

Other bounds remain independent too:

  • Four uploads can still use too much memory if each request reads a large artifact entirely into RAM.
  • An offline producer can fill the disk even when the uploader has impeccable retry logic.
  • A worker can load an enormous queue into memory instead of paging or scanning incrementally.
  • A presigned URL can expire while its artifact waits behind other work.

I treat byte limits, backlog, retention, and scheduling as separate decisions from request count. If the presigned URL for report-0042 expires, the app can obtain a new one and retry using the same report ID.

Choose the smallest complete model

I would start with a directory-backed queue when the workload is single-owner, the backlog is manageable, artifacts are immutable once finalized, and restart recovery can safely retry them. I'd make completion and acknowledgement explicit rather than inferring both from one file's presence.

I would choose a database ledger when the app needs retry schedules that survive restarts, queries over pending uploads, an audit trail, or a safe way for several workers to claim jobs. At that point, refusing the database may be the more elaborate design.

For either choice, I would trace report-0042 through the failure boundaries: production, remote acceptance, durable acknowledgement, and local cleanup. If the process stops between two of those steps, what evidence survives? If the file disappears, is the report lost or recoverable? The answers determine whether recovery retries delivery, retries cleanup, or asks for intervention.

The table count matters less to me than whether I can explain who owns each fact and what recovery does with it.

For this uploader, I'd use file presence for facts the filesystem can establish and persist the facts it cannot. I'd choose the representation that makes those recovery decisions explicit.

1

Maildir is an established example of this pattern: tmp/, new/, and cur/ separate incomplete messages, newly delivered mail, and reader-managed state.

2

I usually dislike encoding application state in filenames or file presence (in-band signalling). But seeing someone else's design persuaded me that this can be a reasonable trade-off for a small uploader.

3

Directories such as rejected/ and acknowledged/ can encode more states through renames. Retry times and errors can also be stored in files; a ledger makes querying and coordinating them easier.

4

On Windows, a scanner or sync client can hold a handle that blocks deletion. Rename guarantees vary too: cross-volume moves may use copy-and-delete.

entry.title: Operating "Systems": Three Uneasy Pieces
entry.content:
Three articles recently forced me to reconsider how I think about constraints and flexibility:1

  • Deliberate Abstraction (Entropic Thoughts) is internally compelling, yet something about its treatment of domain understanding and abstraction bothers me.
  • Sean Goedecke's Make Invalid States Unrepresentable Considered Harmful offers engineering judgment I deeply respect, though I am reluctant to adopt his general preference for fewer hard constraints.
  • Finally, Alex Gaynor's Postel's Law and the Three Ring Circus completely changed my mind about the robustness principle.

I approach these arguments wearing both software-engineering and infrastructure/SRE hats. I’ve worked on legacy systems containing semantically nonsensical data and poorly understood states, though I readily admit I haven't worked at the organizational and service scale that informs some of Sean's conclusions. The central observation tying these pieces together is that both imposing and omitting constraints create costs that can be difficult to identify in advance.

A brief prelude: Epistemology, Data, and Reality

My philosophy on software modeling stems largely from William Kent's Data and Reality, especially its treatment of entities, identity, and the inherent ambiguity of modeling reality. A Hacker News commenter, exceptione, once gave an unusually precise articulation of a modeling heuristic I had independently come to use:

  • Know the problem domain.
  • Think deeply about a conceptual model capturing its relevant aspects.
  • Name concepts carefully because naming feeds back into understanding and modeling.
  • Use a sufficiently expressive language and type system to implement that model.2

The core epistemological problem is that reality does not arrive neatly partitioned into entities, relationships, and invariants. Our models are interpretations shaped by what we need them to do. I try to distinguish evidence from assumptions, conventions, and policies, using domain expertise to inform rather than settle those judgments.3 Even apparently fundamental invariants may just be mistaken assumptions, and modeling is highly iterative—difficulties with naming, representation, and implementation frequently reveal flaws in our understanding. A model is not reality, but that does not make precision in the model unnecessary.4

Piece I—Abstraction and Reality

In conversation with Deliberate Abstraction, there is much the article gets right. Features do not necessarily correspond to components; functionality often emerges from their interaction, and letting a flowchart dictate module boundaries usually produces brittle designs. Modules should hide design decisions, not merely implementation details. Inside-out design can provide general mechanisms for building increasingly specialized layers. Delaying commitments preserves opportunities for change. I recognize two of my biggest influences here: David Parnas on isolating decisions likely to change and John Ousterhout on deep modules that conceal substantial implementation complexity.

Yet a discomfort remains: requirements are not the same as domain understanding. The article argues that changing user requirements make them an unreliable foundation for design. That is reasonable if requirements mean current features, workflows, or implementation prescriptions.

But understanding what users need and why is also our principal means of discovering the domain. Starting with a concrete problem doesn't imply decomposing the software into procedural steps. A deeply understood domain can produce highly general, composable abstractions. We can reject feature-driven decomposition without rejecting problem-driven conceptual modeling.

When the author recommends building around stable fundamentals, we have to ask: which concepts are fundamental? Returning to Kent, identity, classification, and relationships depend partly on how we choose to interpret reality. A supposed domain law might merely be a convention, a policy that depends on the situation, or a mistaken assumption. What appears general may reflect the limits of our current experience.

My interpretation of Parnas and Ousterhout is that deep abstractions should preserve domain semantics, not merely expose generic machinery. The best boundaries frequently follow ownership of knowledge and responsibility.

In Share Resources, Allow Them to Split, I argued that physical co-location must not imply logical coupling. Multiple services can share a database, bucket, or cluster, but each service should own its logical resources and treat their physical placement as an external decision. Sharing a substrate must not grant implicit access to other services' data or internal representations. These boundaries enable sharing, splitting, relocating, or isolating infrastructure as requirements change.

Cross-component operations can become less convenient. Enforcement and testing add work, logical independence does not eliminate physical failure domains, and splitting resources still requires operational coordination. But restricting what a component can know and access can increase flexibility. The value of an abstraction lies in the decisions it isolates, the semantics it preserves, and the changes it enables—not just its generality.

Piece II—In Defense of Constraints, With Reservations

If constraints can preserve optionality, how aggressively should we enforce them when our understanding of the domain might be wrong? Sean Goedecke's Make Invalid States Unrepresentable Considered Harmful argues that some invalid states need to remain representable to accommodate unusual business requirements and operational exceptions. His examples span state machines, foreign keys, and required wire-protocol fields. The disagreement concerns the relative costs and the generality of the prescription.

In the legacy systems I’ve worked on, insufficient constraints have been costly. There are two failures here: invalid states admitted, and unvalidated states trusted. When software admits invalid states, it persists data that contradicts the semantics of the domain. Subsequent writes and computations build upon that data, and inconsistency becomes part of the system's history.

When unvalidated states are trusted, data crosses boundaries into code that assumes guarantees it lacks. Failures occur far from the original problem, leading to difficult diagnosis, manual data repair, and defensive code scattered throughout the application. The absence of constraints does not necessarily eliminate their cost. It can distribute that cost across the system and its future.

In one legacy system, understanding the custom data formats was itself difficult. Just when I thought I understood a rule, another record contradicted it. Fixing that case often broke something else, and some bugs only surfaced much later. Recovering the missing guarantees meant investigation, manual sampling, assertions, and a growing test suite.

Making invalid states unrepresentable (MISU) requires distinguishing three concepts:5

  • Representability: what information the system can retain.
  • Validity: what guarantees a representation establishes.
  • Permitted transitions: what operations can produce or modify that state.

A raw record may be incomplete; a validated domain value satisfies the invariants its type promises; an executable operation may require additional preconditions. These need not use the same representation.

These distinctions matter: unknown is not invalid6, reported is not verified, provisional is not established, and an unexpected future value is not automatically meaningless. Make illegal states unrepresentable at the layer where their illegality is an invariant, without confusing context-specific policies with universal domain constraints.

I find it useful to separate three questions about a contract:

  • Does the boundary reject inputs outside its contract?
  • Does the implementation handle inputs inside its contract?
  • Does the contract represent the right domain semantics?

Those questions concern what a contract guarantees. Exceptional business operations raise a related question: how can an operation depart from the normal transition rules without becoming arbitrary mutation? I agree with Sean that such exceptions need not justify expanding the normal state-transition graph. But they still carry side effects, consistency obligations, and security requirements. Bypassing a transition may violate much more than a status field.

An exceptional operation should have deliberately designed authority, preconditions, postconditions, and observability. Repair operations may need different guarantees from normal operations. Escape hatches can be necessary without becoming unrestricted backdoors.

For example, a normal shipping operation might require recorded payment. An offline-payment path can expose a separate, deliberately authorized operation:

type Pending = { status: "pending" };
type Paid = { status: "paid"; paidAt: Date };
type Shipped = { status: "shipped"; paidAt: Date; trackingNo: string };

declare function ship(order: Paid, trackingNo: string): Shipped;

declare function shipWithOfflinePayment(
 order: Pending,
 proof: OfflinePayment,
 by: Admin,
 trackingNo: string,
): [Shipped, AuditEvent];

The offline path verifies the payment evidence, records the actual payment time, establishes Paid, and can reuse ship. It still needs authorization checks and consistent persistence of the payment, shipment, and audit record; the signature alone does not supply them. This preserves the payment invariant while accommodating an unusual workflow.

Database constraints can be expensive to evolve at scale, but a semantic relationship is distinct from the mechanism enforcing it. Some relationships require referential integrity; others represent historical associations that must survive deletion. SQL schemas are both persistence contracts and possible authoritative enforcement boundaries. Sometimes relaxing database-level enforcement makes sense, but it shifts responsibility elsewhere. The enforcement mechanism depends on the domain's meaning, the deployment architecture, and the consequences of violating the invariant.

External wire schemas often serve software that changes independently, while internal types are generally easier to change together. Required Protobuf fields illustrate how rigid wire contracts make deployment coordination dangerous, but parsers can convert flexible wire representations into strictly validated internal types. Compatibility and validity are distinct properties.

Developing this argument made me realize I'd made an analogous cost-accounting omission in Share Resources, Allow Them to Split. I'd described the cost of preserving operational flexibility as essentially zero. That's too strong: ownership boundaries, configuration conventions, isolation, testing, and foregone shortcuts have costs. Even so, I stand by my experience that their marginal cost is usually small when adopted from the beginning, whereas retrofitting those boundaries is incredibly expensive.

As a developer, I pay for abstraction and implementation complexity. As an infrastructure/SRE engineer, I pay for coupling, inflexible deployments, and opaque failures. The question isn't whether a constraint has a cost, but how that cost compares with the alternatives, including its absence and its later introduction.7

Optionality is not just the number of states a system permits today; it also concerns our future ability to understand and change the system. Sometimes preserving it means introducing constraints; sometimes it means delaying them or choosing a less rigid enforcement boundary. MISU is a useful heuristic, not an absolute.

Piece III—Robustness and the Three-Ring Circus

So far, the discussion has mostly concerned individual applications. But permissiveness can have severe consequences even when an application's internal model remains perfectly valid. This is how Alex Gaynor changed my mind about Postel's Law. I previously agreed with the robustness principle: be conservative in what you emit, be tolerant of what you receive. I believed that validating external input at the system boundary and converting it into trusted internal representations was sufficient.

Gaynor exposed the compatibility ratchet: producers emit nonconforming data, consumers accommodate those deviations, and producers face less incentive to correct their behavior. Deviations gradually become compatibility requirements. Written specifications cease to describe the effective protocol, and new implementations must reproduce undocumented quirks. In a three-ring circus of closed-source producers, open-source consumers, and users seeking interoperability, the easiest maintainer to reach isn't necessarily the one responsible for the violation.

Boundary validation may protect my own application, but it does not prevent the producer's noncompliance from becoming established practice. Individually reasonable accommodations can collectively degrade interoperability, raising the barrier to entry for new implementations and making future protocol evolution harder.

This shares a common pattern with invalid persistent state. Within an application, unvalidated data becomes persistent historical baggage when later code relies on it as though its meaning were established. Across a protocol ecosystem, accepted deviations become compatibility baggage. In both cases, accidental behavior acquires the status of a contract, and the cost of restoring explicit semantics increases over time. Permissiveness can create commitments just as surely as constraints can.

I now think about robustness differently. I distinguish between unknown but permitted extensions, supported schema versions, incomplete information, nonconforming inputs, and information whose meaning I cannot determine.

That means processing what the contract permits and preserving unknown data when the contract permits it, without treating it as validated domain state.8 Malformed semantics call for rejection with useful diagnostics, and quarantine or repair where necessary. Unavoidable deviations need explicit compatibility exceptions; rejection need not mean crashing or an inability to recover.

Robustness means handling deviations without losing control of the system's semantics. I no longer accept liberal parsing as a generally desirable default. When deciding how strict to be, I now consider interoperability, incentives, and ecosystem evolution. I want compatibility workarounds to be deliberate, documented, observable, and limited where practical. The original formulation appears in RFC 761, section 2.10, and RFC 9413 offers a recent critique.

Suppose a wire contract expresses USD amounts as integer cents, but one provider version sends decimal dollar strings:

function parseAmount(raw: unknown, src: Source): Amount | Rejected {
 if (typeof raw === "number" && Number.isSafeInteger(raw)) {
 return minorUnits(raw);
 }

 // Known deviation: provider-x v2 sends "12.50". Reported upstream.
 if (
 src.is("provider-x", "v2") &&
 typeof raw === "string" &&
 isDecimalString(raw)
 ) {
 metrics.count("quirk.provider-x.decimal-amount");
 return fromDecimalString(raw);
 }

 return reject("amount", raw);
}

Here, Source comes from the integration context, not a version claim in the payload. fromDecimalString converts exactly to cents and rejects amounts outside the domain's limits; minorUnits enforces the same limits. The exception accommodates a known wire defect without widening the accepted format for every producer.

Three Uneasy Pieces, No Universal Formula

Our models are necessarily incomplete, our predictions about future requirements are unreliable, and our experience can bias how we estimate engineering costs. Even so, software must make definite decisions and provide guarantees that its users can rely on. For me, the answer is neither to avoid commitments nor to make them irrevocable, but to make assumptions explicit, enforce justified guarantees, and preserve the ability to revise both.9

Notes

Tarasov and Tarasova’s Questions and Answers in School Physics inspired me to try writing this as a dialogue. The article took a different form, but I wanted to acknowledge the inspiration.

It's all epistemology, economics, and emergence.

  • Epistemology: What do we know, and how do we know it?
  • Economics: What does it cost, and what trade-offs are we making?
  • Emergence: What happens when all the pieces interact, often in ways nobody intended?
1

The title is a nod to Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces by Remzi H. Arpaci-Dusseau and Andrea C. Arpaci-Dusseau.

2

When the language cannot express the model's constraints, they may live instead in comments, imperative validation, and developer discipline. This feels like a relative of Greenspun's law: a sufficiently complex project can end up with a half-baked type system of its own.

3

In “On Stupidity”, part of “After Ten Years” in Letters and Papers from Prison, Dietrich Bonhoeffer describes a loss of independent judgment under the influence of power, rather than a lack of intelligence. His context was Nazi Germany. I draw a narrower connection to my own modeling work.

4

Domain-driven design (DDD), strong typing, making invalid states unrepresentable (MISU), information hiding, and deep modules are incredibly useful approaches. Optionality, semantic integrity, comprehensibility, observability, and controllability are the qualities I want to preserve. None of the techniques are ends in themselves.

  • Optionality: the ability to make, defer, or revise decisions later at reasonable cost.
  • Semantic integrity: the faithful representation of reality in the system's data and trusted state.
  • Comprehensibility: the degree to which people can understand what the system does and why.
  • Observability: in the control-theory sense, the ability to infer a system's internal state from its external outputs.
  • Controllability: in the control-theory sense, the ability to drive a system from any state to a desired state through its available inputs.
5

My response to discovering that a distinction is blurry is usually to name three more distinctions.

6

SQL's NULL offers a related distinction: missing information is not the same as an invalid value. Comparisons involving NULL generally yield UNKNOWN, rather than TRUE or FALSE. But NULL alone cannot distinguish “not yet known,” “not applicable,” and “not reported”; when those differences matter, the model needs to represent them explicitly.

7

There's also the question of who pays: a shortcut for the developer may become repair work for the operator, and an operational safeguard may add implementation work. Since I wear both hats, this is partly an argument about which version of me gets the bill.

8

In certain systems, I like having a place where I can chuck quarantine data or raw data. See Paul Gross's Storing External Requests.

9

In an ideal world, I'd like to be rigorous about what my software claims to know, humble about what I might have misunderstood, and deliberate about the costs of both enforcing and relaxing its guarantees.

entry.title: Keeping Things In Sync (Or Why We Can't Have Good Things)
entry.content:
When you have two related pieces of code that need to stay consistent—say, a data structure and its serialization logic, or an API and its documentation—you face a fundamental problem: how do you keep them from drifting apart?

The Cowboy Approach

Just… don't worry about it. Write your struct, write your JSON handler, ship it. If they drift apart, you'll find out in production when a customer complains. This works great until it doesn't, which is usually around 2 AM on a Friday.

The appeal here is velocity. No ceremony, no tooling, no build step that takes three minutes to regenerate files. The downside is that you're essentially gambling that you (or worse, your coworker) will remember to update both places. Spoiler alert: you won't. Someone once widened an int32 to int64 in a C++ parser for Chromium's session history format and missed the corresponding write path. No crash, no assertion—just silently corrupted data downstream that I found by coincidence.

Document It

Write it down! Create a spec, maintain a README, leave a comment that says "IMPORTANT: if you change X, also change Y." This is what professionals do, and it works exactly as well as you'd expect from a system that relies on people reading documentation.

The documentation approach acknowledges that keeping things in sync is important but solves it with process instead of automation. It's better than nothing, which is damning with faint praise. At least when things break, you can point to the document and say "well, it says right here…" We documented the int32/int64 invariant from the cowboy era. An LLM-generated patch missed it, same silent corruption, same broken downstream data.

AST Analysis and Linting

Now we're getting serious. Use static analysis tools to parse your code's abstract syntax tree and verify invariants. Custom eslint rules can enforce that every enum variant has a corresponding case in your handler. Clippy can yell at you when your Rust implementations diverge from expectations.

This catches mistakes before they reach production, which is a meaningful upgrade from the cowboy approach. The limitation is that AST analysis can only check relationships it's been explicitly taught about. You need to write (or configure) the rules, and the tools are only as smart as their rule sets.

Code Tests

Testing is the boring, reliable workhorse of the sync problem. Write tests that verify the relationship between your related pieces of code. If your API handler doesn't match your OpenAPI spec, the test fails. If your database schema doesn't match your ORM models, the test fails.

Tests are great because they're explicit about what should be true, they run automatically, and they prevent regressions. A round-trip test on the session history parser finally killed the int32/int64 bug class for good—we wrote it once and let it be. The downside is that you're maintaining three things now: the original code, the related code, and the tests that verify they match. Also, tests only verify properties you thought to test, which means the creative ways things can desync will surprise you.

Runtime Validation and Contract Testing

Instead of writing separate assertions about shape, define the shape once and make it the bouncer at every door. Zod parses unknown data against a schema at the edge of your system—if the shape is wrong, it fails immediately with a clear error, not three layers deep in business logic. Pact takes this further across services: consumer and provider independently verify against a shared contract, so neither side can drift without the other knowing.

The schema is both the documentation and the enforcement—you can't forget to update the check because the check is the definition. Unlike code generation, you're still writing both sides; you're just guaranteeing they agree on the boundary. The tradeoff is runtime cost and the fact that you only catch mismatches when the code actually executes—a deployed typo in a rarely-hit path can still hide until a user wanders into it six months later.

Derive and Code Generation

Why maintain two things when you can maintain one thing and generate the other? Define your protocol buffer schema and generate code for six languages. Write your database schema and generate your ORM models. Maintain your OpenAPI spec and generate your client libraries.

Code generation takes one source of truth and mechanically produces everything else. When the source changes, you regenerate, and consistency is guaranteed by construction. Go uses this pattern extensively (go generate, protoc-gen-go, sqlc). The tradeoff is that you need to commit to the generator's opinions about what the generated code looks like, and debugging generated code is about as fun as it sounds.

The classic problem: the generated code is either in version control (and your diffs are polluted with mechanical changes) or it's not (and new developers can't build the project without installing seven tools).

Schema Registries

Code generation's bigger sibling: the source of truth doesn't live in any single codebase—it lives in a registry that multiple services validate against. Kafka's Schema Registry enforces that producers and consumers agree on Avro/Protobuf schemas before messages ever hit the wire. API gateways can reject requests that don't match a registered OpenAPI spec. It's like a treaty with actual enforcement mechanisms instead of strongly worded letters.

No single team can unilaterally break the contract. Schema evolution rules (backward/forward compatibility) are enforced centrally, and violations are caught at deploy or publish time, not in production. The tradeoff is infrastructure: you now depend on an external system for correctness, versioning gets political across teams, and local development requires either a running registry or a convincing fake. Also, good luck getting three teams to agree on a schema evolution strategy—you've traded code drift for committee drift.

Auto-Derive and Type-Level Programming

If schema registries solve the problem with infrastructure, this solves it with math. The final boss. Instead of generating code as a separate build step, use the language's type system or metaprogramming facilities to derive implementations automatically. Rust's derive macros mean you add a field to your struct and serialization, comparison, hashing, and debug formatting all update automatically—you literally cannot forget. Haskell's generics let you write functions that work for any type with the right shape. Scala's implicit derivation summons implementations from the type system itself.

This is "code as data" taken seriously. Your types carry enough information that the compiler can figure out how to serialize them, compare them, or hash them without you writing anything. It's like code generation but at compile time, and the generated code is checked by the same type system that generated it.

The downside is that you're now programming in two languages: the surface language and the type-level meta-language. When something goes wrong, the error messages are arcane because the compiler is trying to explain why it couldn't derive a thing you never wrote in the first place. Your build times bloat as the compiler does more work at compile time—Rust projects heavy on derive macros are notorious for this. The tooling struggles too: autocomplete and go-to-definition get confused when half the code doesn't exist until compilation. And this only works in languages with sufficiently fancy type systems, which rules out a lot of mainstream options. This is why we can't have good things—the final boss demands you pay in language complexity, build minutes, and tooling gaps.

Choosing Your Fighter

As you move down the spectrum, you trade manual flexibility for automated consistency. You're deciding where you want the complexity to live—in your discipline and processes, or in your tools and type systems. Neither is free, but at least with tools, the computer can be wrong at 3 GHz instead of you being wrong at coffee-break speeds.

entry.title: Deployment Strategies for Small Teams That Actually Work
entry.content:
Core Principles

  • Hard to Mess Up: Guard against fat fingers and tolerate infrastructure hiccups. A deploy that runs twice should produce the same result, not two versions of a service fighting over migrations in an infinite loop—which is exactly what happened when we accidentally deployed two versions to places that were supposed to be in lockstep, and they ran up and down migrations to reconcile forever. Account for partial failures and transient outages too; the system should absorb mistakes, not amplify them.
  • 2AM Fixable: Clear error messages, obvious rollback procedures, good logging, and simple architecture. The best 2 AM fix is often "revert to the last known good version." Make that trivial to do.
  • Hand-off-able: Standard tooling, few or no clever tricks. Common tasks automated, both SOPs and gotchas documented. A new team member should be able to deploy without a brain dump from the person who set it up.
  • Cost-Conscious: Don't spin up a Kubernetes cluster for a service that runs fine on a single box. Question whether the infrastructure is hiding problems or solving them.

What that means

  • Automated: Manual deployment steps are bugs waiting to happen. Every deployment should be triggered by a single command or git push. No SSH-ing into servers to run commands in sequence. No "remember to restart this service after that one." Automation catches mistakes that humans make when tired or rushed. It also serves as living documentation—the deployment script shows exactly what happens, in what order.
  • Immutable and Declarative: Don't patch running systems—replace them. Build a new image with Docker or Packer, deploy it, tear down the old one. Pair that with a declarative desired-state system that's idempotent: describe what you want, let the tooling converge to it, and run it again without fear of side effects.

Docker Compose/Podman Quadlets on a Single Server

This is my go-to recommendation for teams just starting out or running low-traffic services.

Why It Works

Easy enough to maintain without a dedicated ops person. You get isolation between services, straightforward configuration, and the ability to deploy multiple applications on one box. Perfect for the Hetzner dedicated server or colocation setup that gives you solid hardware at reasonable prices.

The Registry Trick

Here's something teams often miss: chuck your base images and the image layer just before adding your application code into your own registry. This gives you reproducibility and faster deploys. When you need to rebuild, you're not pulling Node or Python base images from Docker Hub every time—you've got them cached in your own registry.

SQLite Is Fine, Actually

For most small team applications, just use SQLite. Seriously. It handles more load than you think, eliminates an entire class of deployment complexity, and makes backups trivial. You can always migrate later if you actually need to, but chances are you won't. The ceiling is when you need multiple app servers or a separated database machine—at that point you've outgrown SQLite and the single-server setup together.

Systemd Services with Proper Isolation

This approach is harder to maintain but works reliably once you've set it up correctly.

You're running your applications directly as systemd services, using systemd's isolation features (DynamicUser, PrivateTmp, ProtectSystem, etc.) to sandbox your processes. No containers, just good old Linux process isolation.

The advantage is simplicity—no container runtime, no image builds, just binaries and configuration files. Systemd's sandboxing features also mean a runaway process can't trash the rest of the system. The disadvantage is that you need to handle dependencies, library versions, and environment setup yourself. This works well for Go or Rust applications that compile to static binaries, less well for dynamic language stacks with complex dependencies.

Nix + Systemd

Nix brings reproducible builds and declarative configuration to the systemd services approach.

Advantages

Complete reproducibility—your entire system configuration is in version control. Atomic rollbacks when deployments go wrong. No dependency conflicts between applications. Built-in development environment matching production.

Requirements

This only works if you have a Nix expert on the team and everyone is willing to learn. The learning curve is steep, the ecosystem is rough around the edges, and I personally haven't been able to justify introducing it to a team. But if you already have the expertise, the reproducibility payoff is real.

Docker Compose for Stateless + Separate Machines for Databases

This is the first step toward separating concerns in your infrastructure.

Why This Works

Your stateless application containers are easy to recreate, redeploy, and scale horizontally. Your databases and storage systems need more care—proper backups, replication, monitoring. By running them on separate machines (or using managed services), you're acknowledging this difference.

The Latency Trade-off

Yes, you've added network latency between your app and database. For most applications, this is 1-3ms on the same provider's network. It's not going to kill your performance, and it's worth the operational simplicity of not having your database container competing for resources with your application.

Container Runners + Managed Databases

This is what I suggest to most teams once they're beyond the single-server phase.

Use services like AWS ECS, Google Cloud Run, or Azure Container Apps for your application containers. Pair them with managed database services (RDS, Cloud SQL, Azure Database). You get automatic scaling, load balancing, and health checks without running Kubernetes.

Cloud Run in particular is excellent for small teams—you pay only for actual request time, it scales to zero, and deploys are straightforward. ECS gives you more control if you need it. Both are dramatically simpler than running your own orchestration.

The managed database is non-negotiable at this level. You don't want to be the one responding to disk full alerts at 2 AM or debugging replication lag.

Kubernetes: The Last Resort (Kind Of)

I list K8s last because most small teams don't need it, but there's a caveat: the ecosystem of Helm charts and operators is genuinely lovely. I spent days trying to set up a Cassandra cluster on bare metal; with a Kubernetes operator I had one running in a few hours, and managing it was dramatically easier. CloudNativePG is another great example. Helm charts and operators encode operational expertise as code in a way that isn't really available on other deployment platforms, and the Kubernetes API makes writing operators straightforward.

If you're deploying standard infrastructure components (monitoring, logging, service mesh, databases for development), this ecosystem can save massive amounts of time. But you're also taking on the operational burden of Kubernetes itself—and that's substantial.

Only go this route if you have specific requirements that simpler solutions can't meet, or if someone on your team already knows K8s well. The complexity tax is real.

Conclusion

Start simple. A single server with Docker Compose will take you further than you expect. Add complexity only when you have specific problems to solve, not because it feels more "professional." The best deployment strategy is the one your team can actually maintain at 3 AM when something breaks.

Refs

  • Simple Made Easy — Rich Hickey
  • A Conjecture on Why Reliable Systems Fail — Lorin Hochstein. Reliable systems tend to fail because of manual interventions meant to fix minor incidents, or unexpected behavior of subsystems designed to improve reliability.
  • Choose Boring Technology

entry.title: Things I've Come to Believe In: A Technical Stack Confession
entry.content:
These aren't religious convictions—I won't argue about them at parties (maybe at KubeCon)—but they've proven themselves reliable enough that I reach for them by default.

Driving Principles

  • No complexity cliff: Simple things should be easy. You should only pay the complexity cost that you need. I watched a system that should have been a single service get split across multiple services communicating over a message bus—none of it necessary. Debugging a request became an archaeological dig, and deploying without breaking a consumer became nearly impossible. Introduce complexity progressively, when you hit a concrete wall, not before.
  • 2 AM Fixable and Handoff-able: You can fix it half-asleep and hand it off to the next person without a brain dump. We self-hosted GitLab once. Someone deleted a live database because it was named badly and protected worse. A managed service wouldn't have prevented all human error, but it would have absorbed the class of failure we spent that morning firefighting.
  • Cost Conscious: Not just "keep the bill low"—question whether the infrastructure is hiding problems. We moved a low-traffic deployment from standard Kubernetes to k3s on a single node of the same instance type. Cost dropped, but that wasn't the real win—latency went down and throughput went up because the extra networking layers and hops had been adding overhead, and autoscaling had been quietly masking bad tuning for months. The bill was a symptom; the disease was complexity we weren't using.
  • No toil: The aspiration, at least. Automate the repetitive stuff even if you never reach zero. It used to take a full day to get a new cell ready, and it broke in new ways each time because someone forgot a step or accidentally introduced one. I tried automating it, but the automation couldn't keep up with the service sprawl. The toil problem and the complexity cliff problem fed each other.

Containers

2 AM Fixable, No toil

Containers solved the "works on my machine" problem, and I'm never going back. The ability to ship an application with its exact runtime dependencies is transformative. (I use Nix btw. Yes, I'm that person. No, my config isn't "almost done."1)

CI/CD

No toil, No complexity cliff

Automated testing on every commit catches bugs before they metastasize. The feedback loop tightens. You stop treating "deploy day" as a special event requiring sacrifice to the ops gods. Whether to automatically deploy is a case-by-case call—depends on security requirements, maturity of the service, and how much you trust the test suite. Either way, keep HEAD deploy-ready and make deploys a one-click thing. Good CI makes shipping boring—which is exactly what you want.

Single Page Applications

No complexity cliff, Cost Conscious

Hosting and caching are easy. Append a SHA to your built CSS/JS and cache them indefinitely. Set up your index.html file with a small TTL. And you're sorted. No fiddling about with Vary to make sure a tenant doesn't see another's data—server-rendered multi-tenant apps risk CDN cache poisoning if you get the Vary header wrong, serving one tenant's page to another. The cost is complexity and initial bundle size, but shrugs23.

Postgres as Primary Database

No complexity cliff, 2 AM Fixable

We used unlogged tables as a cache layer, regular tables for longer-lived caches, and SKIP LOCKED for job queues—all without standing up Redis, Memcached, or a dedicated message broker. That's three fewer systems to monitor, back up, and explain to the on-call engineer at 2 AM. Postgres might not win benchmarks against purpose-built databases, but it absorbs an enormous number of use cases with less operational overhead4567.

Modular Monoliths and Modes

No complexity cliff, 2 AM Fixable

The part I like most about a modular monolith is runtime modes: the same codebase can run as an API server, background worker, or scheduled job processor just by toggling which modules initialize. Expose your REST endpoints on an instance in API mode, run it as a background queue consumer in worker mode—all from the same Git repo and deployment artifact.

A modular monolith organizes code into well-bounded modules within a single deployable unit—the structural discipline of microservices without the distributed systems headache. Enforce module boundaries through namespace conventions or architectural tests (ArchUnit is your friend here), and use dependency injection to wire modules together while preventing circular dependencies.

DevEx

The DevEx win is substantial: developers can run the entire application locally with a single docker-compose up or even directly, eliminating the "wait, which seven services do I need running to test this?" problem.

Testing becomes dramatically simpler since you can spin up the whole system in-process for integration tests without mocking HTTP boundaries or dealing with flaky container orchestration.

Using a batteries-included framework like Spring Boot, Django, or Rails for the monolith is a force multiplier here—you get auth, ORM, migrations, admin, and background job infrastructure for free, so you can focus on your domain logic instead of reinventing plumbing.

Configuration

When configuring runtime modes, stick to positive feature toggles like ENABLE_API_SERVER=true and ENABLE_BACKGROUND_WORKERS=true rather than negative ones like DISABLE_WORKERS=false, because double negatives make your configuration files read like a boolean logic puzzle8.

Satellite Services

No complexity cliff, 2 AM Fixable

Microservices sound great until you're debugging distributed transactions across twelve repos. Keep a main application backed by satellite services for concerns that truly benefit from separation.

We handled ML and data analytics workloads in Python alongside the main app—attempts to migrate them into the monolith were painful, and adding features later even more so. We once had an RCE on a mixed workload running user templates; life would've been easier if untrusted code had been separated by a network boundary. I've rewritten small proxies that filter and shape traffic for slower monoliths when the gateway got too complex, and spun off latency-sensitive parts of Rails monoliths into Rust or Go.

The common thread—separate when:

  • Taking advantage of an ecosystem that isn't present in your main language
  • Running highly sensitive operations
  • Running untrusted code
  • Compute-bound workloads that benefit from a faster runtime
  • Latency-sensitive operations that need a leaner service

API Gateway

No complexity cliff, 2 AM Fixable

We had enterprise customers complaining about whitelisting two endpoints. We had six, some unavoidable. A gateway centralizes authentication, rate limiting, request routing, and response transformation—bringing that endpoint count down significantly. Kong, AWS API Gateway, Traefik—pick one that matches your scale. But the real value is the escape hatch: when a service has a long-term issue or a short-lived bug, the gateway gives you room to work around it—rewrite a path, shed load, inject a header—without touching the service itself. That's the kind of lever you want at 2 AM9.

The Pattern

The problems feed each other: service sprawl creates toil, toil resists automation, hidden complexity masks bad tuning. The principles aren't independent—violate one and the others start to crack.

Look at the tags above. "No complexity cliff" shows up everywhere—that's the through-line. I don't want simple things to be hard, and I don't want to pay for complexity I'm not using. "2 AM Fixable" is a close second: most of these choices make systems easier to reason about when you're half-asleep and on-call. Cost consciousness and no-toil round it out—keep the bill sane, automate the drudgery.

The principles also pull against each other. Self-hosting is cheaper, but managed services are easier to fix at 2 AM—cost consciousness and operability trade off directly. Automation eliminates toil, but the automation itself becomes a system to maintain—sometimes the toil is cheaper than the complexity of eliminating it. And investing in automation has an upfront cost; for low-frequency tasks, the automation might never pay for itself.

None of these technologies, processes, or perspectives are perfect10. But they're good enough that I can stop relitigating the same architectural arguments and get back to work11.

1

I use Nix for personal projects, but its flakiness (pun intended) and complexity made it a no-go for introducing to the team.

2

But seriously—the real cost: larger initial bundles, client-side routing complexity, SEO gymnastics, and accessibility pitfalls that server-rendered HTML handles for free. These are real trade-offs, not minor inconveniences.

3

Some newer server-rendering frameworks, combined with CDN caching, make it surprisingly easy to leak one tenant's data to another. In a SPA, the auth boundary lives in API calls you already have to get right. In server-rendered multi-tenant apps, every response is a potential leak surface.

4

ACID compliance, JSON support, full-text search, geospatial queries, powerful indexing, mature replication—Postgres keeps absorbing features that would otherwise require specialized databases. Need a queue? Use SKIP LOCKED. Need pub/sub? Built in. Need time-series data? Extensions exist.

5

Rails is moving in this direction too—Solid Queue, Solid Cache, and Solid Cable all bet on the database as the single backing store.

6

The exception that proved the rule: we switched to ClickHouse for heavy time-series analytics. It's a fantastic database for that job, and knowing where Postgres stops reinforced how far it stretches everywhere else.

7

SQLite deserves a mention here—for single-node deployments and embedded use cases, it carries the same philosophy of "one database, fewer moving parts" even further.

8

Negative flags also create awkward coupling: you end up in situations where you can't enable a feature you want without disabling something else first.

9

I wrote more about sharing a single resource and splitting later in Share Resources, Allow Them to Split.

10

This list is intentionally scoped to the things I have strong opinions on. Observability, infrastructure as code, feature flags—all important, none ready for my "I'll die on this hill" list yet.

11

Choose Boring Technology

entry.title: Share Resources, Allow Them to Split
entry.content:
There's a quiet design principle that pays for itself many times over in microservice architectures:

Share infrastructure resources where you can. Write services as if you weren't.

The two halves of the principle pull in different directions on purpose:

  • Sharing is what you do at deployment time, to keep operational cost and complexity down.
  • Splitting-readiness is what you do at design time, to keep your future options open.

A service that's been written correctly doesn't know or care whether its bucket, its database, or its domain is shared with five other services or entirely its own. That ignorance is the feature. This is a specific instance of the rule behind Bezos' famous API mandate: all service communication goes through published interfaces; everything else—shared memory, direct linking, back doors—is forbidden. Two services sharing a bucket is an operational convenience; one service knowing it shares a bucket is a coupling that bypasses the service contract.

The setup: two services, one bucket

Suppose you have two microservices—say, an invoicing service and a reporting service—and both need to write files to S3. The naïve options are:

  1. Give each service its own bucket.
  2. Put both in one bucket and let them write wherever.

The first is wasteful. Buckets aren't free in operational terms—each one is a thing to provision, secure, monitor, lifecycle, back up, audit, and pay for. If you have forty microservices, you do not want forty buckets when ten will do.

The second is a different kind of mess: collisions, accidental overwrites, no clean way to apply per-service IAM policies, lifecycle rules, or replication.

The right answer is to share the bucket but prefix the keys:

s3://company-data/invoicing/2026/05/invoice-1234.pdf
s3://company-data/reporting/quarterly/q1-2026.pdf

Now both services share a single piece of infrastructure, but their data is cleanly partitioned. IAM policies can scope invoicing/* to the invoicing service and reporting/* to the reporting service. Lifecycle rules can target one prefix and not the other. Replication, encryption, observability, cost attribution—all of it can be applied per-prefix. The bucket is shared; the concerns are split.

The same idea applies to API gateways and load balancers:

https://api.company.com/invoicing/...
https://api.company.com/reporting/...

One domain, one TLS certificate, one DNS record, one load balancer—but two cleanly separated services. This is the share half of the principle.

The other half: don't assume the sharing

Here's where most teams quietly create future pain. The invoicing service is configured to write to s3://company-data/invoicing/.... The reporting service is configured to write to s3://company-data/reporting/.... So far, so good.

The mistake is letting the code know that both services use the same bucket.

You see this when:

  • A shared utility library hardcodes the bucket name and only takes a prefix as input.
  • One service reads files written by another directly out of the same bucket, assuming co-location.
  • A deployment script provisions one set of bucket-level credentials and hands them to several services.
  • An engineer writes a cross-service feature that does ListObjects across both prefixes in one call.
  • Documentation and runbooks refer to "the data bucket" rather than "the invoicing service's bucket."

Each of these silently couples the two services to the same bucket forever. The day you want to move reporting to its own bucket—perhaps because it's grown large enough to justify dedicated lifecycle policies, or it now lives in a different AWS account, or compliance demands isolation, or it needs to be replicated to a different region—you can't. Not without a refactor.

The fix is straightforward but disciplined: each service treats its bucket and prefix as opaque configuration. The invoicing service doesn't know there's a reporting service. It doesn't know whether its bucket is shared or dedicated. It just knows: "here is my bucket, here is my prefix, write here."

# invoicing service config
storage:
 bucket: company-data
 prefix: invoicing/

# reporting service config
storage:
 bucket: company-data
 prefix: reporting/

Today, both bucket values happen to be the same. Tomorrow you change one, redeploy that one service, and nothing else needs to know.

The pattern, stated more carefully

Stripped of S3 specifics, the principle has three parts:

  1. The substrate is the shared resource. A bucket, a domain, a database server, a Kafka cluster, a Redis instance, a Kubernetes cluster, a metrics backend.
  2. The namespace is the per-service partition within the substrate. A key prefix, a path prefix, a schema, a topic prefix, a logical database number, a Kubernetes namespace, a metric prefix.
  3. The service code knows only its own fully-qualified location —substrate plus namespace, treated as one opaque configured value. It doesn't know the substrate is shared, and it doesn't know the names of any other services' namespaces.

Get those three right and sharing becomes a deployment-time optimisation rather than an architectural commitment.

More examples of the pattern

The same shape repeats almost everywhere infrastructure can be shared. A handful worth seeing explicitly:

Databases

A shared PostgreSQL server with one schema per service. The invoicing service connects with credentials that grant access only to the invoicing schema. Whether it writes INSERT INTO invoices ... or INSERT INTO invoicing.invoices ... doesn't matter—both are fine. What matters is that it never writes JOIN reporting.something. The schema-qualified name is its own address; the problem starts when someone uses it to reach across into a sibling's schema. When invoicing outgrows the shared server, you provision a dedicated database, change the connection string, and the SQL is unchanged.

Kafka and message brokers

A shared cluster with per-service topic prefixes: invoicing.invoices.created, reporting.reports.generated. The service is told its prefix; it doesn't know the cluster has any other tenants. Cross-service communication happens through published events on well-known topics, not by sneaking into another service's prefix.

Redis and caches

One Redis instance, with each service using a key prefix or a logical database number. The service uses keys like user:123:session internally; the prefix invoicing: is added by the client library based on configuration. If you later move invoicing to its own Redis cluster, the keys don't change.

Kubernetes clusters

A shared cluster with one namespace per service or per team. RBAC, network policies, resource quotas, and pod security all attach to the namespace. Services have no notion of the cluster's broader topology—they're configured with their own service URLs and don't reach across namespaces by hardcoded names.

Observability backends

A shared Prometheus, Grafana, or Datadog instance with per-service metric prefixes, log indices, and trace service names. Dashboards and alerts are scoped per service. When one service's volume justifies a dedicated backend, it moves; nothing else changes.

The same shape appears in CDN routing (path-based origins), secrets management (per-service vault paths), and CI/CD pipelines (per-service artefact paths and credentials). In every case the recipe is the same: a shared substrate, a per-service namespace, and code that knows only its own fully-qualified location.

The same principle, one level in

The pattern isn't limited to infrastructure shared between services. It applies just as well within a single service, between tenants.

Share the database. Partition every row by tenant_id. Write queries as if each tenant's data lived in its own database—because one day, for your largest customer, it will. Many SaaS companies eventually do exactly this: the big customer gets a dedicated database, a dedicated cluster, sometimes a dedicated region.

The rule is the same: share the substrate, namespace the contents, keep the code oblivious to the sharing.

One config value or two?

A common question: should the service receive the substrate and namespace as two configuration values, or as one composed string?

Two values is fine:

storage:
 bucket: company-data
 prefix: invoicing/

One composed value is better:

storage:
 location: s3://company-data/invoicing/

The real rule has nothing to do with one value versus two. The real rule is: don't magick. Don't strip the prefix to "discover" the underlying bucket. Don't construct paths into another service's namespace. Don't write utility code that takes a prefix and assumes everything lives in the same bucket. Don't log the components separately in ways that invite someone to reassemble them. Two config values are perfectly fine as long as the service treats them as its own coordinates and never uses them to reason about the broader infrastructure.

What you actually buy

This costs nothing on day one and saves enormous effort by year three. Concretely:

  • Operational flexibility. When one service's storage, traffic, or data shape diverges from the others, you split it out by changing config and redeploying that one service. No coordinated migrations, no synchronised cutover.
  • Blast radius control. Sharing infrastructure means a misconfiguration or noisy neighbour can affect every tenant. If splitting is cheap, you split the moment you have a real reason—a security incident, a compliance requirement, a performance anomaly. If splitting is expensive because code assumes co-location, you live with the risk far longer than you should.
  • Honest service boundaries. When code knows it's sharing a bucket with another service, the temptation to reach across—"just read it directly, it's right there"—is enormous, and engineers will succumb under deadline pressure. Treating the location as opaque kills the temptation at the source. Cross-service data access goes through APIs and events, as it should.
  • Cleaner local development and testing. A service that doesn't assume any particular shared infrastructure can be pointed at a local stack, a per-developer sandbox, or a CI ephemeral environment with no code changes. The same binary runs everywhere from laptop to production.
  • Clearer cost attribution. Per-namespace tagging, per-prefix metrics, and per-schema billing become straightforward when each service genuinely uses only its own slice. You can answer "how much does invoicing cost?" without untangling shared data.
  • Easier acquisitions, spinoffs, and migrations. When a service has no hidden dependencies on its substrate, moving it—to a different cloud, a different account, a different company—is mostly a configuration exercise. Hidden assumptions are what make these migrations gruelling.
  • Simpler on-prem and customer-managed deployments. When you ship software to a customer's environment, every resource you need is a line item in a provisioning request. Asking for one Postgres instance and one S3-compatible bucket is a conversation; asking for ten of each is a multi-week back and forth. Sharing keeps the resource footprint small enough that on-prem deployments stay practical.
  • Faster dev and test environments. The same logic applies to developer laptops and CI. One database and one bucket spin up in seconds. Ten of each is a docker-compose file that takes a minute to start and breaks in new ways every month.
  • Cell-based architectures. When services are indifferent to whether their infrastructure is shared or dedicated, you can mix and match cell topologies freely. A small cell runs everything on shared infra. A large cell gives hot services dedicated resources. A customer cell gets full isolation. The same service binaries deploy to all three—only the configuration differs.

When sharing is the wrong default

Not everything should be shared. Some resources should be separate from day one:

  • Data at different sensitivity tiers. PII, payment data, and authentication secrets deserve dedicated infrastructure not because sharing is technically impossible but because the blast radius of a misconfiguration is unacceptable. A leaked IAM policy on a shared bucket can expose data from every service in the prefix tree. This goes double when regulation explicitly mandates isolation—HIPAA, PCI-DSS, FedRAMP—where sharing creates legal exposure on top of technical risk.
  • Wildly different access patterns. A service that does millions of small reads per second and a service that does nightly multi-terabyte batch writes should not share a database or a storage backend.

The principle still holds in these cases—write the service as if the resource could be shared, even when you know it won't be. The discipline of opaque configuration costs nothing. You're just choosing to start on the "split" side of the spectrum rather than the "shared" side.

A checklist when introducing a new shared resource

When you introduce a new shared resource, work through these:

  • Does each service have its own prefix, schema, topic, or namespace within the shared resource, with no overlap?
  • Is the full path (substrate plus namespace) externalised as opaque configuration, not fiddled with inside the service?
  • If you changed one service's config tomorrow to point at a separate resource, would anything break? If yes, what assumption is hiding?
  • Are cross-service interactions going through APIs and events, never through direct reads of another service's namespace?
  • Do per-namespace IAM, network, lifecycle, and observability policies actually exist, so that the capability to split is real and not just theoretical?
  • Do your runbooks and documentation refer to resources by service ("invoicing's bucket") rather than by shared name ("the data bucket")? Language shapes thinking.

If you can answer those cleanly, you have the best of both worlds: the efficiency of shared infrastructure and the freedom to split it the moment splitting is worthwhile.

The principle, finally

Share the substrate. Namespace the contents. Keep the service oblivious to the sharing.

Sharing is a deployment-time choice you make to save cost and complexity. Splitting is a future deployment-time choice you preserve by writing the service correctly today. The two are not in tension—they're the same decision viewed from different time horizons.

The services that age well are the ones whose code is indifferent to whether they're sharing or alone. They were always going to be one of the two; you just don't have to decide now, and you don't have to decide forever.

entry.title: Autocorrect helps unravel what little is left of my sanity
entry.content:
I’m the world’s most frustrated man,
My brain is fried, my thumbs are weak.
I thought more AI would solve my problem,
But now the outlook’s rather bleak.
Give me a pen, a piece of paper,
A stick, a rock, a bit of clay;
The duck king Autocorrect never understood,
The things I actually wanted to say.

Omakes:

> I thought more AI would solve my problem,
> But it crushes the words I speak.

> I thought more AI would solve my problem,
> But my Microsoft Outlook is now bleak.

entry.title: Scripting For Profit
entry.content:
Scripting?

Scripts are everywhere, from doing backups of your DB server to S3, listing all the namespaces in a Kubernetes cluster without pods, or simply bootstrapping your environments. A day doesn't go by without writing a new script or at least executing a script I wrote before.

Scripts make life easier. They save time on repetitive tasks. They are ubiquitous.

Having been writing scripts for a while 1, I wanted to write an article to:

  • pen my thoughts and opinions on scripting 2 for "production" (after all, the article is titled "…For Profit");
  • maybe help others (including my future self) by documenting some good scripting hygiene and common pitfalls in one place. 3

Shell Scripting on Linux

If you are writing scripts on Linux, you are probably writing them in a Shell scripting language (Bash, mostly). Even if you've used Python, Ruby, or Node, you've probably still written a Shell script or ten—either out of convenience, or because nothing else was available. The appeal of scripting in Shell probably comes from how you use the same constructs in the interactive commands you run in the Terminal and how easy it is to glue several commands together.

The gluing constructs shell provides (everything-as-text and pipes) mean that if your program is oriented around "commands", nothing beats it 4 5. Shell is an excellent Domain Specific Language that is failure tolerant (to a fault) and concise (again to a fault).

Bashing Bash

There are several excellent reasons not to use Bash. Some of the oft-cited reasons are:

  • It is stringly-typed: Almost all bash variables are strings.
  • Arcane incantations: Bash usage is full of abstruse invocations like $*, $#, and <() (process substitution). Short arguments and obscure built-ins are both hard to read and hard to google.
  • Awkward syntax: The syntax differs significantly from other popular languages.
  • Have to use tools: Bash doesn't have a standard library; it relies on external tools, which can be inefficient and inconsistent across systems.

  • Environments can differ: The tools you want may not be installed on your target system, or a subtly different version may behave unexpectedly.

    • BSD vs GNU anyone? 6

Why use Bash?

  • Ubiquitous: Bash is available in almost all Linux environments. (Even if Bash isn't available, a POSIX-compliant shell likely is.)
  • Powerful: Pipes and the Unix culture of small, composable tools make everyday automation easy.

Better Bash

When not to use Bash

A part of writing good Bash scripts is knowing when to reach for other tools 7. Consider something other than Bash when:

  • Your script is longer than a few hundred lines.
  • You need rich data structures like hash-maps or nested lists.
  • You have a hard time working around quoting issues.
  • You do a lot of string manipulation or arithmetic.
  • You do not have much need for invoking other programs or pipelining them.
  • You worry about performance or need complex control flow (e.g. nested loops).

What to use instead:

  • Python: Great syntax and standard library; lacks native YAML support (a pain for DevOps).
  • Ruby: Has YAML in the standard library and elegant shell integration. Best when you control all target systems.
  • Perl: Powerful text processing; less common today.
  • zx / bun shell: JavaScript-based scripting with a modern feel.
  • Golang: Excellent for distributing statically compiled binaries that run anywhere.
  • Language of your choice: People have used Go, Rust, Haskell 8, C, and Java 9 for scripting.

  • Alternative shells: There are also alternative shells worth knowing about, though I don't personally reach for them — if I'm installing a new tool anyway, I'd rather switch to a full language.

    • Nushell treats pipeline output as structured data — tables and typed values — rather than raw text, so you can write select login contributions instead of piping through jq.
    • Oil Shell takes a compatibility-first approach: its OSH mode runs existing Bash scripts as-is, while YSH layers a cleaner language on top, giving a gentler migration path for legacy scripts.

If I want to replace a bash script, I use Python, Ruby, or Golang. Python is my first choice unless I have to deal with YAML; in that case I use Ruby (for scripts that only run on systems I control) or Golang (for anything else, since I can hand out statically compiled binaries).

Some reasons you may still prefer Bash:

  1. You are largely dealing with filesystem operations such as moving, copying, and deleting.
